item.title: A Lesson From Germany
item.description:
Over the past few weeks, Donald Trump has been negotiating a lot of potential business deals with Vladimir Putin. His administration has discussed lifting sanctions, including on Moscow’s flagship government investment fund; in some cases, that’s already happened.

What’s going on? Some see favoritism toward an autocrat Trump has seemed to admire (and an attempt to lower U.S. fuel prices before midterm elections tomorrow.) The administration argues that it’s all part of a broader effort to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.

For me, as a German, it’s all a bit of a déjà vu. When I was Berlin bureau chief a few years ago, I wrote a lot about Germany’s longstanding policy of trying to influence Russian behavior with business and energy deals. Even after Moscow invaded Crimea, Berlin approved another major gas pipeline. The policy was abandoned only after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Today, I write about the lessons of Germany’s failed Russia policy for the Trump administration.

First, there was the potential Lukoil deal.

Last month, my colleagues reported that the Trump administration wanted a U.S.-led consortium to buy the international assets of one of Russia’s biggest energy companies.

Next, the administration waived some U.S. sanctions to buy Russian diesel and leaned on Europe to resume buying Russian gas. Then we learned that it considered a proposal to buy Russian technology to gain access to and liquefy natural gas in Alaska.

Now, it’s exploring yet another concession: lifting sanctions on Russia’s flagship government investment fund.

Trump wants to end the war in Ukraine. He has repeatedly tried and failed. His latest approach, spearheaded by the two businessmen who are his main negotiators — Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, his son-in-law — is aggressively focused on offering Putin economic incentives.

Witkoff and Kushner have argued that the prospect of doing business with the West could persuade the Russian president to compromise in Ukraine.

So far, however, it’s not working. Putin is happily banking all of the concessions while not making any of his own.

The idea of tempering Russia’s behavior with economic incentives isn’t new, nor is it inherently implausible. In fact, it’s the approach Germany took for decades, with, at least for a while, meaningful success.

But it stopped working for Germany for the same reason most experts think it won’t work for the United States now: There are things Russia cares about more than business deals.

Ostpolitik

Until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, there was a shared belief in Germany — embraced by a long succession of chancellors, industry leaders and the public — that a Russia bound by trade would have too much at risk to enter into a conflict with Europe. Doing business with Russia, the thinking went, was a win-win: It would make Germany safer and richer.

That policy had its origins in the Cold War, when the West German government ushered in a new policy of engagement with the Soviet Union that became known as Ostpolitik. Ostpolitik was a broad philosophy that included other aspects of the relationship, too — diplomacy, cultural contact. But one of its defining pillars, which only grew in importance over time, became known as “Wandel durch Handel,” or “change through trade.”

I spoke to Liana Fix, who wrote a book about Germany’s evolving Russia policy. Ostpolitik helped build trust between the two sides, particularly during the Cold War, she said. The gas pipelines constructed from the 1970s onward might have made the end of the Cold War more peaceful.

But at the time, gas deals were accompanied by deterrence. “The other piece of it was missiles pointing at Moscow,” Fix said.

That changed after the Cold War. A reunified Germany cut military spending. At the same time, it intensified its business and energy ties with Moscow.

Initially, there was a belief that these ties would help transform post-Soviet Russia into a liberal democracy, Fix told me. But even when Germany’s political establishment became disillusioned with Putin, it still held on to the belief that mutual interdependence would make it too costly for him to step out of line.

It kept believing this after the invasion of Crimea in 2014: Angela Merkel persuaded Barack Obama not to ship arms to Ukraine and instead approved Nord Stream 2. Germany had leverage over Russia, the thinking went, precisely because it was buying so much Russian gas.

The opposite turned out to be true. It was Putin who restricted the flow of gas, in 2021. The next year, he invaded Ukraine.

Lessons from the past

The U.S. does not share Germany’s tortured history or, for that matter, a continent with Russia. And it will never be strategically dependent on Russian gas in the way Germany was until very recently.

But if Trump’s goal is to end the war, one thing the German experience shows is that Putin is motivated by things other than business deals. This has been an incredibly costly war for Russia and Putin has shown that he’s prepared to pay the price.

Not everyone agrees about why Putin invaded Ukraine. Some, like Stephen Walt at Harvard, argue that what incited Putin was the offer of a path toward NATO membership extended to Ukraine in 2008. Walt pointed me to the memo the U.S. ambassador to Moscow at the time, William Burns, sent to Washington that year, warning that “Ukrainian entry into NATO is the brightest of all red lines for the Russian elite (not just Putin).”

“From knuckle-draggers in the dark recesses of the Kremlin to Putin’s sharpest liberal critics, I have yet to find anyone who views Ukraine in NATO as anything other than a direct challenge to Russian interests,” Burns wrote.

Others, like Fix, say that even in the absence of that offer, Putin’s longstanding imperial ambitions in Ukraine mean he most likely would have invaded anyway.

But people with very different views of what is motivating Putin still agree on one thing: business deals won’t be enough to lead him to give up. And worse, they could enable and embolden him.

The later years of Ostpolitik might be better remembered not for the ways Germany influenced Russia, but for the ways Russia influenced Germany. Former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder, a personal friend of Putin’s, earned millions promoting Russian energy interests. (Read my post-invasion interview with Schröder here. It’s a profile of him, but also of Germany’s Russia policy.)

Now it’s the Trump administration that’s talking to Russia about energy deals. The consortium seeking the multibillion-dollar Lukoil deal includes an American investor who is a Trump donor, Middle Eastern business executives with ties to Witkoff and Kushner, and an arm of the U.S. government itself.

For more: When will Russians finally be fed up with the war? My colleague Valerie Hopkins asked some of them what they thought.

If you have questions about how Russians view the war, send them to us here.

item.title: China’s Message to Its Rivals: You Need What We Make
item.description:
They are among the biggest machines in the world: steel cylinders, some as long as a football field, armed with rotating discs that can chew through rock to clear the way for roads and railways. Known as tunnel boring machines, they are made by only a handful of companies, mostly in factories in China.

India uses them to dig tunnels, including in the Himalayas, to improve its ability to send troops to defend its contested border with China. But starting next month, Beijing is likely to be able to control whether India gets to buy them.

The machines are part of a broader effort by China to control what leaves Chinese factories and laboratories for foreign lands. In the past month, Beijing has moved to control the exports of dozens of technologies, including drones, artificial intelligence models and agents, and certain processes used to develop advanced medicines and to make solar panels.

The overall push could make it much harder for companies in the United States and elsewhere to set up solar energy equipment factories that would compete against Chinese manufacturers. And it could soon make it more difficult for anyone outside China to gain access to the latest and most powerful Chinese A.I. models.

The planned restrictions show that Beijing is doubling down on its strategy of making Chinese factories indispensable to the world, even as many governments are alarmed by their countries’ dependence on China and are pushing to be less reliant.

In the United States, concern over China’s grip on rare earths has spurred the government to revive the country’s own mining and processing industry for the minerals. In Europe, Japan and elsewhere, governments are trying to reclaim their ability to make antibiotics and active ingredients of medicines, many of which now come from China. In India, the transport minister has urged companies to make tunnel boring machines locally.

For Xi Jinping, the Chinese leader, the controls are the realization of a plan he laid out years ago, when the pandemic exposed China’s dependence on foreign countries for advanced medical equipment like ventilators and life-support systems, as well as for raw materials and specialized parts.

He declared that China would develop “trump card” technologies in industries such as high-speed trains, renewable energy and telecommunications. That would make China not only more self-sufficient, but deter countries from trying to cut China off.

Mr. Xi has depicted China as locked in a long struggle with the West, which he sees as trying to contain China’s rise.

Beijing needs leverage to ensure that China can still get what it needs from other countries — namely their customers and advanced technologies like jet engines and high-end chips, said Kirsten Asdal, a founder of Asdal Advisory, a consultancy that focuses on Chinese political research.

“Xi and the party see themselves as naturally embattled” against the West, she said, and have been “angling for a confrontation sooner or later, whenever the opportunity and capability present itself.”

At home, the Communist Party has framed China’s push for industrial and technological might as a fight for survival, echoing the struggles of the party’s revolutionary past.

In recent days, the party has repeatedly invoked the Long March, the Red Army’s epic 6,000-mile strategic retreat that cemented Mao Zedong’s leadership and became its defining myth of triumph over impossible odds. By drawing on that history, the party may be trying to reassure ordinary Chinese that endurance under its leadership will carry China through a time of slower economic growth, a prolonged housing crisis and growing hostility abroad.

In a recent front-page editorial commemorating the 90th anniversary of the Long March, People’s Daily, the party’s mouthpiece, called for the country to “focus on the ‘chokehold’ key core technologies” and “stiffen the Chinese backbone” of self-reliance.

In a clear reference to the United States, the editorial praised China for weathering tariffs and trade wars and urged readers to prepare for a “great struggle.” The call to secure technological choke points was also likened to the way the Red Army took the “strategic initiative” on the battlefield to ultimately defeat the Nationalists.

China has said that the recent flurry of export controls and proposed rules are needed to protect Chinese business interests. The country has spent decades and billions of dollars developing its dominance of the manufacturing of solar equipment, for instance, and it argues that it must restrict the export of core equipment to prevent competitors from trying to replicate China’s supply chain domestically.

China has also said that more controls are needed to guard against threats to national security.

“China is beginning to more systematically consider which technologies and equipment can be exported, to whom they should be sold and what their ultimate applications will be,” said Sun Chenghao, a foreign relations expert at Tsinghua University in Beijing.

He said, for instance, that the risks that A.I. could be used for cyberattacks or that machines that bore tunnels and that dredge mud could be used by militaries against China are legitimate reasons for Beijing to vet where these technologies go.

The proposed controls may also be a part of tit-for-tat actions that China and the United States have traded in recent months, despite a broader trade truce. The Trump administration added BGI, a major Chinese genomics company to a trade blacklist aimed at barring products made with forced labor in China. Earlier, the Treasury Department proposed regulations prohibiting U.S. companies and investors from taking investment stakes in Chinese biotechnology firms.

President Trump and Mr. Xi are expected to meet in China later this month and next month in Miami.

American restrictions and sanctions on China helped teach Beijing that great powers need economic weapons as much as they need aircraft carriers and long-range missiles, some analysts have said. Washington first cut two of China’s largest technology companies, Huawei and ZTE, off from American chips and software, then restricted exports of advanced chips to China broadly, curbs that continue to hurt China’s A.I. ambitions.

During its trade war with the second Trump administration, Beijing choked off exports to the United States of rare earths, the minerals needed to make fighter jets, cars and everyday technologies. That pressured Washington into a truce.

Some Chinese analysts worry that Beijing’s rare earths strategy has been too successful. The United States and many of its allies and partners are now scrambling to develop alternative sources.

Part of this month’s flood of Chinese controls was aimed at establishing new points of leverage.

“China is concerned that it might lose its ‘rare earths card,’” said Zhao Minghao, an international relations scholar at Fudan University in Shanghai. “So, what other cards does China still hold? How can China effectively counter U.S. sanctions or tariff measures? I believe Beijing is prioritizing this highly at the present.”

China’s single-minded focus on technological self-sufficiency carries risks for Beijing.

Economists have long urged Beijing to invest in pensions, health care and unemployment benefits so that residents feel secure enough to spend.

“That obsession with developing technology and protecting it is leading to a massive misallocation of resources in China that is generating slower growth and higher debt,” said Scott Kennedy, a researcher on the Chinese economy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington.

The new controls could also alarm other trading partners like Europe, which is already uneasy about a flood of cheap Chinese exports.

“That kind of business by threat is not going to be something that is sustainable,” Mr. Kennedy said.

Even some Chinese analysts acknowledge the danger.

“If uncertainty becomes too high, customers may seek alternatives,” Mr. Sun of Tsinghua said.

That is already happening in India. Experts say that China had been holding up exports of tunnel boring machines as early as 2024, before it added them to its list of export controls. As a result, India has had to seek out other suppliers.

Yet New Delhi had few ways to retaliate because its economic ties with China were so thin, said Pranay Kotasthane, chair of the High Tech Geopolitics Program at the Takshashila Institution in Bengaluru, India.

“China is indiscriminately expanding the scope of their export controls to include basic equipment that aren’t even strategic,” he added. “They are demonstrating that in any political conflict, they can counter with industrial leverage.”

item.title: A Canadian Sketch Show Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
item.description:
Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.

Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.

In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.

For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.

“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharias.

“The show’s been on a long time, and we can be the butt of the joke sometimes as far as what people think our demographic is,” she said. “But in the six seasons I’ve been here, more young people are coming up to us who love it and watch it all the time.”

The characters Ms. McGunnigle most likes to play are pro-life, pro-gun, pro-war and pro-push-up bra. “Too much makeup, no moral compass, a pathological desire to protect the patriarchy, and blonde. Terrifying!” she said.

The show, which airs Tuesday nights on the publicly funded Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, leans progressive but traffics in nonpartisan political satire — anyone in the headlines is fair game. Since Mr. Trump began his second term, the show routinely points its lens at the United States and its deteriorating relationship with Canada.

“This Hour Has 22 Minutes” is the nosy neighbor with permanently raised eyebrows.

Fans include Graydon Carter, the Canadian-born former editor of Vanity Fair and co-founder of Spy magazine.

“Canadians are feeling an uncharacteristic blush of patriotism,” he said. “And there’s nothing like friction and impending chaos to bring out the satirists.”

Ms. McGunnigle operates with fast-twitch newsroom instincts. As soon as Ms. Zacharia held her first disastrous White House briefing, she knew the show had to do something. “And that 14-minute press conference,” Ms. McGunnigle said. “I felt we weren’t going to have her for long.”

While they were shooting the piece a few days later, Ms. Zacharia was fired. Ms. McGunnigle immediately began improvising, turning a sketch about Ms. Zacharia’s disastrous first news conference into one about her last. A bonus: “Saturday Night Live” was dark that week.

“Stacey McGunnigle’s Katie Zacharia was superb,” Mr. Carter said. “But for her it was a bit like getting the coveted lead in a play that closes on opening night.”

The weekly broadcast averages 571,000 viewers, up 31 percent from 435,000 last season, with 25- to 54-year-olds the leading demographic. The “Meet Katie” sketch has more than 21.5 million views across social media, and the first Leavitt sketch more than 7.8 million.

Mark Critch, a veteran cast member and writer in his 24th season, plays Mr. Trump.

“We’re the quiet house next door, and the house on the other side of the fence, they have a lot of loud parties, and there’s always arguing in the yard,” he said. “We’re watching over the fence going, ‘Oh, my God, what’s going on?’ We get to observe, which is a good thing for comedy.”

Mr. Critch has taken his Trump to Greenland. He whipped up a “Quiet, Piggy” sketch after the president insulted a reporter with the phrase. As Mr. Trump, he fulminated over The New York Times’s exclusive interview with Prime Minister Mark Carney, in a cold open. In an attempt to rekindle Canada-U.S. relations Mr. Critch, as himself, met with Gov. Janet Mills of Maine, who implored him to ask Canadians to resume visiting her state.

“I mean God almighty,” he said, “Even with all the arguing that goes on, there’s nothing a Canadian gets excited about more than American attention.”

Drawing inspiration from the Trump administration isn’t entirely new for the show. What is more recent is the speed at which the show reacts to news. Without social media, the show, taped on Mondays, would struggle to stay timely on Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States.

“TV shows are big machines and you don’t want to be late to the party,” Mr. Critch said. “There’s another audience that we can get to right away. When something happens in the moment, now the whole building pivots.”

Mike Allison, the executive producer and showrunner, said more people tuned in as Canadian-U.S. tensions escalated. Especially amusing has been the opportunity for interplay between Mr. Trump and Mr. Carney, played by Mark McKinney, on the war in Iran, reverse psychology, and McDonald’s. But not every sketch needs a Canadian tie.

“When writers pitch Kristi Noem or Kash Patel, that’s us looking over the fence at all the crazy characters running the country,” Mr. Allison said. “But U.S. politics have become Canadian politics.”

“22 Minutes has the DNA of the knowing outsider,” Mr. Carter said.

It always has. Twenty-five years ago, “Talking to Americans” was a popular segment testing how little Americans knew about Canada. Highlights included a Columbia University professor agreeing that the government should stop putting senior citizens on ice floes to die, and Mike Huckabee, then the governor of Arkansas, congratulating Canada on preserving its national igloo.

Mr. Critch often hears from Americans who don’t realize the show is Canadian.

“They will say, ‘Oh, good, thank you. That’s what I feel.’ But then you’ll get some saying, ‘You don’t know anything! That’s our president! Shut up!’” he said. “Something I see that’s actually very Canadian is Americans saying they’re sorry. ‘I’m so sorry this is happening. I’m so sorry they’re saying these things about your country. We love Canadians.’”

item.title: Syria Weighs Joining Saudi Mutual Defense Pact as Yemen War Rages
item.description:
Syria is considering joining a regional defense alliance with Saudi Arabia, its foreign minister said on Saturday, raising the prospect that Damascus could become involved in the kingdom’s widening conflict with the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen.

Asaad al-Shaibani, the Syrian foreign minister, told the Manama Dialogue security conference in Bahrain that “discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” referring to a mutual-defense pact signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.

Under the terms of the pact, known as the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, an armed attack on any of its three members would be considered an attack on all, mirroring NATO’s collective-defense principle. The countries agreed this month to prepare for the rapid deployment of military forces to Saudi Arabia as the Houthis have intensified their attacks on the kingdom.

Mr. al-Shaibani said that Syria regarded the defense of Gulf Arab countries as essential to its own security. “Syria will stand beside all of the Gulf countries,” he said, adding that they faced challenges from “militias that cross borders.”

It was unclear, however, whether that potential support would extend to sending Syrian troops to Yemen.

Since sweeping to power almost two years ago, President Ahmed al-Sharaa of Syria has sought to stay out of regional conflicts, as his government has struggled to rebuild the country after nearly 14 years of civil war. The Syrian authorities denied reports this month that Saudi Arabia had requested that Syrian troops be deployed, saying Damascus was focused on reconstruction.

But Syria’s growing ties with Saudi Arabia could complicate that position, analysts say. Saudi Arabia has become a major diplomatic and economic supporter of Syria since the country’s longtime dictator, Bashar al-Assad, was overthrown by rebels led by Mr. al-Sharaa. The Assad family, which ruled Syria with an iron fist for more than five decades, had been closely allied with Iran, Saudi Arabia’s regional rival.

This month, Mr. al-Sharaa met with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, in Riyadh, where they discussed investment and regional security, according to a statement from the Syrian president’s office.

Syria has raised the possibility of joining the defense pact as fighting in Yemen and attacks on Saudi Arabia have intensified after years of relative calm.

After the Houthis seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, in 2014, Saudi Arabia began a disastrous bombing campaign the following year in support of the country’s internationally recognized government. The fighting largely subsided after a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022, but it has escalated this year amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

The renewed fighting has killed at least 1,677 people and wounded more than 7,300 in Yemen since August, according to the World Health Organization. Nearly 300,000 Yemenis have been displaced, the United Nations has said, deepening a devastating humanitarian crisis in one of the world’s poorest countries.

In Saudi Arabia, Houthi missile and drone attacks on airports and vital infrastructure have killed at least 19 people and wounded hundreds more, according to the Saudi-led military coalition. The escalating attacks, which have severely disrupted air travel, have increasingly threatened the kingdom’s ambitions to become a global tourism and business hub.

As the attacks have intensified, Egypt — which is not part of the Mecca pact — this week authorized military aid to Saudi Arabia, another sign of the growing regional response to the conflict.

On Saturday, the Saudi-backed coalition said it intercepted three drones over the kingdom, including one near the capital, Riyadh. In Yemen, six people, including three children, were wounded in what the Houthi authorities said was a Saudi airstrike on a grocery store in Taiz Province.

Taiz, one of Yemen’s largest cities, has become a major battleground in recent weeks. The Houthis have cut road access to the strategically located city, leaving its residents with dwindling supplies of food, water and fuel.

Taiz is at a crossroads between Houthi-held territory in the north of the country and the government-controlled south and the Red Sea coast. Taking control would help the Houthis increase pressure on government forces and cement control of coastal areas on the Red Sea.

In another development, the Houthis have come under renewed scrutiny for arresting a number of U.N. personnel and aid workers two years ago. On Saturday, the United Nations said that Mohammad el Shami, a Yemeni employee of its human rights office who had been detained since June 2024, had died in custody.

Volker Türk, the U.N. human rights chief, called for an independent investigation into his death.

item.title: Clashes Erupt Again in France, After Festive Start to Day of Protest
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of people poured into the streets of French cities again on Saturday for protests that began with the festivity of a Halloween parade but gave way to darker scenes of clashes between demonstrators and the police.

The violence fell well short of the arson and looting that engulfed Paris and other cities on Oct. 17, when a mass demonstration muted into widespread lawlessness. The crowds, estimated by the government at 320,000, were also smaller than on the previous two Saturdays of nationwide protest.

Still, the turnout — and the chaos — was significant enough to suggest that France remains in the grip of acute unrest, nearly two months into a protest movement that began with rebellious high school students.

In several cities, the police fired tear gas and sprayed water cannons to disperse some protesters after what had been peaceful rallies. In Paris, 200 to 300 rioters, masked and clad in black, skirmished with police officers into the evening, lobbing Molotov cocktails, fireworks and other projectiles.

It was a discordant end to a day that had begun on an upbeat, even joyful, note. Many people made the most of the fact that the demonstration coincided with Halloween. They showed up in eye-catching costumes, as Spider-Man, Zorro or the Pink Panther, dancing as often as they marched. One, dressed as Marie Antoinette, held a sign that said, “Let them eat cake.”

French officials had said they worried that the holiday would introduce a dangerous element, since demonstrators might conceal their faces. They marshaled 70,000 police officers, the same number as last week, and shifted routes to keep the protesters away from city centers.

France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, condemned what he said were violent rioters, with links to the far left, who mixed in with the protesters. Many of them broke into clashes with the police as the marches ended and the authorities tried to disperse the crowds.

On Saturday evening, Mr. Nuñez said, the police in Paris were still confronting “groups that intend to head to the Bastille,” the site of an uprising in 1789 that is a milestone in the French Revolution. The Paris authorities had prevented the march from starting there.

“The intent is to create an insurrectionary climate — a quasi-revolutionary atmosphere — and to attack domestic security forces in order to gain access to stores, to carry out looting, to attack public buildings, and they are attacking law enforcement in an extremely violent manner,” Mr. Nuñez said.

In Paris, television images showed the police coming under attack by fireworks and Molotov cocktails. At least one officer was briefly engulfed in flames, an attack that Mr. Nuñez said qualified as attempted murder. Trash bins were set alight, as was a car. Similar chaotic scenes played out in Marseille, Rennes, Nantes, Toulouse, Montpellier, Angers and Tours.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader and presidential candidate, condemned the targeting of police officers, writing on social media that the “perpetrators of this attack must be found and sentenced with the utmost severity.”

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a far-left leader who is also running for president, accused the government of undercounting the crowds. He claimed they were as large as previous demonstrations, despite the change in the route.

The police arrested 565 people, which Mr. Nuñez said prevented a worse outbreak of violence. The authorities also carried out 40,000 spot checks across the country to prevent people from taking weapons to protest areas.

But Mr. Nuñez was careful not to declare victory. The Interior Ministry warned that the violence could intensify long after darkness fell. On Saturday night, bands of people still roamed Paris and other cities. “We will remain vigilant throughout the evening and the night,” he said.

It was a stark contrast to earlier in the day, when people began massing for the marches. Brass bands played music, and the protesters’ costumes provided a celebratory atmosphere. Several people said they wanted to help reverse the narrative set on Oct. 17, when the marches mutated into violence, with gangs smashing shop windows and looting the contents.

“I’m really worried about how the riots have been instrumentalized by the far right,” said Helen Olive, 50, who was among a group of parents who had dressed as “super parents.” “We want to turn that narrative around.”

Arthur Fleury, a 20-year-old literature student, came as a prisoner riding a dinosaur and wearing a mask of Ms. Le Pen, the far-right leader. “Protests are about making demands but also having fun,” he said. “I was going for an absurd costume to capture the spirit of the movement.”

As the crowd marched along its route in eastern Paris, a bystander dropped candy from his balcony, drawing cheers. But there were already signs of trouble. Half a dozen masked protesters in black pushed trash bins, one of which was burning, into the middle of the crowd. They set a second bin on fire near where a police unit was stationed.

Other demonstrators used water to put out the fire, precipitating a small clash with the masked group. “That’s no way to protest,” said one of those who helped put out the fire.

Among the protesters were Morgane Voisin, 22, and Corentin Schnell, 19, both of whom wore white outfits identifying them as “street medics” able to deliver first aid. Ms. Voisin, a sales consultant, said she participating because her younger siblings had faced harsh conditions in high school.

Mr. Schnell, an engineering student, said he joined after his younger brother told him he was tear-gassed and almost struck by a stun grenade at a protest this month.

“The mere fact that people are being injured by the police makes me furious,” Mr. Schnell said. “So, I’ve come to demonstrate and to try to provide medical care — to limit the damage, regardless of which side it’s on.”

On Saturday, the two said they saw one person who had been injured in the head. Help arrived quickly. “Long live youth!” Ms. Voisin said.

Giulia Imbert contributed reporting.

item.title: He’s the Top Snake Catcher, and Business Is Booming. There’s Just One Problem.
item.description:
Once you see a snake in Bangkok, the snakiest capital in the world, you see snakes everywhere. Loops of electrical wire look like snakes. Gas pump hoses look like snakes. Vines, green and vibrant, look like snakes.

There are also, as Pinyo Pukpinyo knows, a lot of actual snakes. In Bangkok each year, about 30,000 snakes are caught by fire and rescue personnel. On an average half-day shift, Mr. Pinyo, the top snake catcher in Thailand’s capital, wrangles more than 20 snakes, the reptiles secreted in sewers, curled in flowerpots and toilets, enmeshed in recycling, and pressed against branches ready to snack on geckoes and tree shrews.

He catches cobras, pythons, kraits and pit vipers. Those are the scary snakes. Harmless species, at least to humans, include tree snakes, rat snakes, kukris and sunbeams.

Mr. Pinyo, 56, who joined Bangkok’s fire department at 18 only to discover that firefighters here do a lot more snake catching than firefighting, wants one thing known above all else: He does not kill the snakes he catches.

Part of it is his Buddhist faith. But mostly it’s that it’s not the snakes’ fault that we humans have spread our urban jungle into actual jungle. It’s not the snakes’ fault that Bangkok floods during the monsoons, drowning their cozy habitats and forcing them to swim past malls and condominiums.

“They deserve to return to nature,” Mr. Pinyo said. “They only bite when they’re forced to defend themselves.”

This principled ban on snake extermination has left Mr. Pinyo with a problem, one that has multiplied in the months since his Bang Khen fire station in northeastern Bangkok, now under renovation, moved to a few prefab structures squeezed under an elevated monorail.

Mr. Pinyo has way too many snakes.

He is not sure how many, but it’s more than 200. Or it could be 300. It’s definitely 70 cobras. At least. In his concrete cavern of a fire station, the sun blocked by the Skytrain’s tracks, nearly every tub, every water bottle, every sack, every plastic container that might otherwise hold shoes or bedsheets, is home to a snake, sometimes multiple snakes. Some of the pythons measure 15 feet long.

Every few months, Mr. Pinyo drives out of Bangkok and unloads a horror movie tangle of snakes in a national park or forest. Then he starts again, catching and collecting snakes until it’s time for another rural pilgrimage.

Feeding all of these snakes costs about $300 a month, money that comes out of Mr. Pinyo’s pocket. His wife and daughter do not like snakes. His father, who died this year, was so upset by all of the venomous snakes that he refused to visit Mr. Pinyo when he was hospitalized with the inevitable snakebite. But snakes, Mr. Pinyo says, chose him. It is his karma.

“My father used to say that I’m stubborn, like a cobra,” Mr. Pinyo said. “Maybe it’s true. I had to learn everything myself and stick to it because no one taught me how to catch snakes.”

Mr. Pinyo’s father, a hotel limousine driver, wanted his son to land a stable government job, and Mr. Pinyo passed the police examination. But a chronic shortage of firefighters meant he was assigned to that career instead. His starting base salary was less than $100 a month. (He now makes about $1,500.) He admits he was terrified when dispatched, without any training, to catch his first python, armed only with a stick with a hook at the end.

“I wanted to catch bad guys like in the movies, not catch snakes,” he told me.

He learned fast on the job. He studied books like “The Manual of Practical Management of Snake Bites and Animal Toxin Injury.” Along the way, he discovered that as much as he liked divining the personalities of snakes — the way a cobra mimics a human’s movement or the way a baby python practices its bite — what he really enjoyed was the reaction of humans newly relieved of snakes in their homes or offices.

“They offer me many prayers and good wishes,” Mr. Pinyo said. “It’s better than what money can buy.”

Like a doctor at a dinner party burdened with the ailments of fellow guests, Mr. Pinyo is constantly called upon for his expertise. Luckily, he is generous. I shared my snake stories. In 2019, I had put a Post-it note on the door of my home office in Bangkok, warning the boys not to bother me because I was on a call. My husband had done the same. Our younger son, then 9, rapped anyway.

“Mama,” he said, “I’m sorry, but there’s a pit viper in the dining room.”

Our son was right: There was a snake in our living room, a flash of fluorescent green. I disregarded my husband’s Post-it note, and he grabbed a bucket and pasta tongs. The snake, though, exited onto the balcony on its own.

I showed Mr. Pinyo a photograph of my husband, armed with the tongs, ready to tackle the snake. He praised my husband’s choice of tool, but said our son had been wrong. It was not a pit viper. There was no streak of red near the tail.

“Only a tree snake,” he said. “No danger.”

Last month, Mr. Pinyo and his deputy snake catchers conducted a training at a Mövenpick hotel in Bangkok, the lobby carpet plush and the garden lush. Like anywhere in Bangkok, there were snakes, and everyone, from the concierge and duty manager to spa therapist and room cleaner, needed to be prepared.

The firefighters had brought 50 live snakes with them, and believable scenarios unfolded in the underground garage. Let’s say there’s a small cobra and all you have is a small water bottle.

With differing levels of terror, the hotel workers caught small cobras in small water bottles. They caught medium-size cobras in medium-size water bottles. They simulated a situation in which a snake lurks in the shower and all there is to work with is a towel. (“Please don’t open your towel and scare the snake,” Mr. Pinyo joked.) The workers took turns as impromptu matadors, gently laying the towels on cobras with their hoods raised, ready to strike.

By the end, it felt perfectly natural to think that we could all be snake catchers. My colleague Muktita Suhartono had refused to touch a snake, but under Mr. Pinyo’s supervision, she coolly decanted a golden cobra into a plastic bottle, screwing on the lid after checking that the animal’s head was nowhere near the spout.

Still, there’s a reason there are snake professionals. Mr. Pinyo has been hospitalized four times for near deadly snakebites, the last time for two months. He insists he can’t even remember how many times he’s been bitten in total.

I mentioned that my husband was bitten by a pit viper last year. After an emergency room stay, he was on crutches for weeks. Mr. Pinyo made a sympathetic noise, but then said he never seeks medical care for something as trifling as a pit viper bite. Yet a younger colleague of his became functionally paralyzed after a cobra bite during a training not so different from the one we attended.

One day in October, Mr. Pinyo sat on a plastic stool underneath the train tracks at the makeshift fire station. Occasionally, a sack shifted ominously. A hiss or rattle emanated from a box. Then the calls came: a snake in a pile of recycling, a snake in a hollow bathroom door, a snake at a medical clinic. We pulled up to the clinic, where young people were standing on a ramp at the entrance. They scattered when Mr. Pinyo asked if this was the place with the snake under the ramp.

He pulled up the ramp to find a reticulated python twisted into a misshapen pretzel. The python went into a sack, and we drove back to the fire station, with one more snake to feed and release into the wild.

“Circle of life,” Mr. Pinyo said, his fingers forming a loose loop like a python at rest.

Muktita Suhartono contributed reporting.

item.title: Mass Protest Expected in New Delhi Over Modi and Voter Roll Changes
item.description:
Tens of thousands of demonstrators are expected to converge on India’s capital on Sunday in a display of mass resistance to the government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and recent changes to the voter roll.

The event, organized by India’s largest opposition political party, the Indian National Congress, will be the latest in a string of large protests to ripple through New Delhi since this summer.

The demonstrators have marched under different banners, with separate leaders and demands. But they have all expressed unhappiness with Mr. Modi’s nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, which has led India since 2014, and its initiative to update India’s voter rolls. The protesters have accused Mr. Modi of “vote theft,” claiming that his party is using its powers to try to rig the rolls in its favor.

“B.J.P., Modi — all are trying to demolish our rights, our constitution,” said Mohammed Shamin, 40, a private tutor from Delhi who planned to attend. As he mingled among the several hundred people who had started to gather at the demonstration site in central New Delhi on Saturday evening, Mr. Shamin said he was optimistic that their presence would make a difference.

“Every cloud has a silver lining,” he added, gesturing to the early arrivals and the large empty field behind them that organizers expected would be crammed by morning with people from all over India.

Organizers have said they expect as many as a million people to attend, but police officials have provided a much lower estimate of 50,000. Laborers worked through the night on Saturday to prepare the open-air venue, which was still waterlogged from heavy rain earlier in the week.

The revision of India’s voter rolls began last year in what the government has described as a routine effort to eliminate duplicates, dead people and other discrepancies. It has amounted to a sweeping overhaul, with more than 130 million names expunged so far.

Millions of people have said they were included in the purge by mistake, leading critics of Mr. Modi and the B.J.P. to accuse him of tampering with India’s electoral system and undermining the fundamental mechanism of its democracy ahead of elections in several large states next year.

Mr. Modi and his allies in the B.J.P. say their political opponents are looking for an excuse to foment unrest, which began in force in July under the banner of the Gen Z-led “cockroach” movement. The Cockroach Janta Party — named as a satirical response to a comment from India’s chief justice about “youngsters like cockroaches who don’t get any employment” — first mobilized young people across India to protest the government’s mishandling of important student entrance exams.

More recent protests have focused on the voter rolls and have largely been led not by the cockroach movement, but by the Congress party and its leader, Rahul Gandhi, the scion of India’s most illustrious political dynasty.

Sudhanshu Trivedi, national spokesman for the B.J.P., on Saturday called the Congress party’s efforts a failed attempt to “to create anarchy in India.” The B.J.P. has called its own counterprotest on Sunday and vowed to combat what it called “the falsehoods, conspiracies and unrest engineered by a desperate opposition.”

Security forces and police officers responded to the earlier protests by locking down the heart of New Delhi, detaining protest leaders and rounding up demonstrators by the thousands. The Delhi police have assigned thousands of personnel to cover the event.

Hari Kumar contributed reporting from New Delhi.
